client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to, because all I can think about is that she's not there. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I should try something.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and reaching out, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that kind of courage matters. I can hear in your voice a quiet, almost restrained sadness, like you're carrying something heavy but trying to hold it together, and that makes complete sense given how recently you lost her. What you're experiencing at those family gatherings — that ache of her absence in a space where she used to belong — is a very real and valid part of grief, not a sign that something is wrong with you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, it almost makes it harder to hear — like, if it's valid and normal, then why does it feel so unbearable? At the last family dinner, my cousin was laughing and telling stories, and I just sat there feeling like I was behind glass, completely disconnected from everyone. I kept thinking I should be able to join in, and then felt guilty for not being able to.
therapist: That image of being behind glass is so vivid and painful — and the fact that your voice carries this soft, almost muted quality as you describe it tells me this disconnection isn't just a thought, it's something you're feeling in your whole body. The guilt you're adding on top of the grief — that "I *should* be able to join in" — is actually a second layer of pain you're creating for yourself, and CBT would call that a thinking trap, because grief doesn't follow a schedule or a rulebook. What if, instead of measuring yourself against your cousin's laughter, we gently explored what it might look like to just *be* at that table, without requiring yourself to feel a certain way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying about the "should" being a trap, and part of me gets that intellectually, but I'm not sure how to actually do what you're describing. Like, what does "just being at the table" even look like when every corner of that room reminds me of her — her chair, the dishes she used to bring, even the way certain people laugh like she did? It feels less like a thinking problem and more like the whole environment is just... saturated with her absence.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with a kind of urgency — tells me this isn't abstract for you, it's pressing and immediate, even as underneath it there's something that sounds almost exhausted, like you've been trying to think your way out of something that lives deeper than thoughts. You're absolutely right that this isn't just a thinking problem — when grief is woven into the physical world around you, every chair and dish and laugh becomes a reminder, and that's not a cognitive distortion, that's love with nowhere to go. So rather than trying to *not* notice those things, what if we explored what it might mean to let those reminders be there — her chair, her dishes — as connections to her rather than only as evidence of her absence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That reframe — "love with nowhere to go" — actually hit me in a way I wasn't expecting, and I had to just sit with that for a second. But I'm also a little skeptical, because in the moment, when I'm actually sitting at that table, I don't know if I'll be able to consciously think "this is a connection to her" rather than just feeling that gut-punch of loss. It sounds almost too gentle for how sharp the pain actually is.
therapist: That skepticism is actually really important and worth honoring — you're not looking for a pretty idea that dissolves the moment it meets real pain, and I hear that. The goal isn't to think your way through the gut-punch in the moment, but rather to practice this perspective now, in quieter moments, so it slowly becomes part of how your mind and body recognize those reminders — less like a conscious thought you have to reach for, and more like a reflex that builds over time. The sharpness of the pain you're describing tells me how deep the love was, and we're not trying to soften that — we're trying to give it somewhere to land.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The idea of practicing it in quieter moments makes more sense to me than trying to apply it in the middle of a family dinner, I'll give you that. But I'm realizing I don't actually have many quiet moments with her memory that aren't also painful — even when I'm alone, I'll catch myself starting to reach for my phone to call her, and then that wave hits all over again. I guess I'm wondering what a "quieter moment" with her even looks like now that she's gone.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — softly, almost gently, like you're handling something fragile — tells me that even asking this question is tender work, and I want to honor that. That moment of reaching for your phone to call her is actually one of the most quietly devastating parts of losing someone close, and it's also, in a strange way, a doorway — because that impulse *is* a quieter moment with her, one where your love for her surfaces naturally before the grief catches up. What if we explored making space for small, intentional versions of that — not to avoid the wave, but to be with her memory on your own terms, like looking at a photo or holding one of her objects, so the connection isn't always arriving as a surprise that knocks you over?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: There's actually one thing of hers I have — a small ceramic dish she kept on her kitchen counter, and I took it after she passed without really knowing why. I've mostly kept it in a drawer because every time I look at it I don't know what to do with it, like I'm afraid of what it'll bring up. I guess what you're describing is taking it out of the drawer, but that feels both right and terrifying at the same time.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, quickly, with a kind of breathless quality — tells me that even naming this dish out loud took something out of you, like part of you is bracing for what comes next. The fact that you took it without knowing why is so significant, because some part of you *knew* it mattered before your conscious mind caught up — it wasn't random, it was love making a decision. You don't have to take it out of the drawer today, but when you feel ready, maybe the first step isn't doing anything with it at all — just letting it sit on a surface where you can see it, and letting yourself get used to it being present, the way you're slowly getting used to her being gone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That last part — "getting used to her being gone" — I don't know, something in me resists that phrase, like getting used to it feels like a betrayal somehow, like I'm accepting something I don't want to accept. But I also know I can't keep the dish in a drawer forever, that feels wrong too, like I'm hiding her. Maybe I could try putting it out somewhere, just in my own space, not at a family gathering where everything is already so loaded.
therapist: Your resistance to that phrase is worth listening to — you're not trying to get used to her being gone, you're learning to carry her with you, and that's something very different. The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like your heart is moving faster than you want it to — tells me you've actually just found something important on your own: that putting the dish out in your own quiet space, away from the weight of family gatherings, feels like the right-sized first step, not too much and not too little. That's not acceptance of losing her — that's you finding a way to let her belong somewhere again.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: "Letting her belong somewhere again" — that actually feels closer to what I want, even if I'm not sure I fully understand it yet. I think I could try putting the dish out on my nightstand or somewhere in my room, somewhere that's just mine, not shared with anyone else's grief or expectations. I'm still a little scared of what it'll bring up when I see it every day, but I think the hiding is starting to feel worse than the facing.
therapist: The way you're speaking — with that high, almost luminous quality in your voice, steady and measured — tells me something has quietly shifted in this conversation, like you've moved from being overwhelmed by the question to finding your own answer. What you just said — that the hiding is starting to feel worse than the facing — is a profound and hard-won insight, and it came entirely from you. Putting the dish on your nightstand, in your own space, on your own terms, is a real and meaningful step, and the fear you still feel alongside that decision doesn't mean you're not ready — it means you're doing something that matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I came in here not really expecting to get anywhere, and I'm a little surprised that I actually feel slightly less stuck than when I walked in. I'm still scared about what happens at the next family gathering, though — like, putting the dish out in my room feels manageable, but I don't know how to carry any of this into those shared spaces where other people's grief and expectations are also in the room. That part still feels very unresolved to me.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me that even as part of you feels that small but real sense of relief, another part is already rushing ahead to the next hard thing — and that's okay, that's not you losing what you just found. What you've done today is actually the foundation for those shared spaces: you've started building a private relationship with her memory that belongs to you, and you can bring *that* — not a perfect script or a reframe you have to remember — into the next family gathering. We don't have to solve the shared spaces today; let the dish on the nightstand be enough for now, and we can return to the rest when you're ready.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think you're right that I was already jumping ahead, and I notice I do that a lot — like if I can just figure out all the hard parts in advance, maybe they won't hurt as much when they come. Letting the dish on the nightstand be enough for now sounds simple, but I'm a little worried that between now and the next time we talk, I'll either avoid putting it out at all or I'll do it and then spiral and not have anyone to talk to. I guess I'm realizing I don't have a lot of people in my life I can actually share this kind of thing with, and that feels lonelier than I expected to admit out loud.
therapist: The way you're speaking — very quickly, softly, at a high pitch — tells me that last admission about loneliness caught you a little off guard, like it surfaced before you had a chance to manage it, and I want you to know that what just came through was something really important and brave. That pattern of trying to think through all the pain in advance is such a human way of trying to protect yourself, but you've just named something underneath the grief that deserves its own attention — not just the loss of your grandmother, but a loneliness that was perhaps already there. Before our next conversation, if you do put the dish out and the wave comes, I want you to have one small thing to hold onto: you don't have to process it alone in your head — you could write down, even just a sentence or two, what came up, so it has somewhere to go until we can talk again.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
